Vestibulodynia

Two small sham-controlled PBM trials found short-term reductions on some provoked-pain measures; neither showed a clear advantage for sexual function or perceived overall improvement. A mapped uncontrolled study of mixed vulvar/vaginal pain cannot establish a PVD-specific treatment effect.

Publications and records

2direct RCT publications in the exact category (n=64; Canada and Israel)

Publication and study types

Mapped broader vulvar/vaginal pain evidence: 1 retrospective cohort (n=52; France)

External syntheses: 2 (2022 PVD systematic review; 2026 vulvodynia network meta-analysis)

No cohort overlap identified

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Lev-Sagie 2017: 14/18 (78%) vs 7/16 (44%) reported clinical pain improvement at end of treatment (p=.042); the difference was not reflected across other pain measures. Eight treated participants reported lasting improvement at one year (Lev-Sagie et al., 2017).

Antonio 2025 (endpoint one week after session 15; active n=16, sham n=14): pressure-pain threshold 196.4 +/- 152.2 vs 127.7 +/- 51.4 g; tampon-test NRS (0-10) 2.0 +/- 1.6 vs 3.3 +/- 2.4; VPAQ pain sensations (0-4) 1.7 +/- 0.5 vs 2.3 +/- 0.7. Reported between-group differences across assessments were 28.2-112.0 g (d=.61), 0.1-2.5 NRS points (d=.60), and 0.1-0.9 VPAQ points (d=.87). Sexual function, perceived improvement, and satisfaction were not significantly better (Antonio et al., 2025).

Mapped 2026 mixed vulvar/vaginal pain cohort (uncontrolled; not PVD-specific): 27/52 (52%) met PGI-I 1-2 after six to eight sessions. This is descriptive, not a comparative effect estimate (Plumasseau et al., 2026).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term local provoked-pain measures

Low for perceived overall improvement; very low for sexual-function effects

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two small sham-controlled PBM trials found short-term reductions on some provoked-pain measures; neither showed a clear advantage for sexual function or perceived overall improvement. A mapped uncontrolled study of mixed vulvar/vaginal pain cannot establish a PVD-specific treatment effect.

Summary of the Evidence

Two direct sham-controlled PBM RCTs were identified in provoked vestibulodynia (PVD), enrolling 34 and 30 participants. They used different protocols and pain measures; no cohort overlap was identified. A separate 2026 retrospective study was mapped from mixed vulvar/vaginal pain and is not included in the PVD trial count. A 2022 PVD-specific systematic review and a 2026 vulvodynia network meta-analysis add context but do not create more PBM-specific RCTs.

Human and clinical evidence

In the 2017 pilot, one self-reported clinical pain-improvement outcome favored laser (p=.042), but other measured pain outcomes and sexual satisfaction did not show clear between-group differences; eight treated participants reported sustained improvement at one year (Lev-Sagie et al., 2017). A PVD-specific systematic review found no significant difference for pain during intercourse, pressure/touch pain, or sexual satisfaction in this trial and rated each outcome very low certainty (Bohm-Starke et al., 2022).

The 2025 sham-controlled trial found greater improvement with PBM on pressure-pain threshold, tampon-test pain, and the pain-sensations domain of the Vulvar Pain Assessment Questionnaire. It found no significant between-group differences in sexual function, overall perceived improvement, or satisfaction (Antonio et al., 2025).

A mapped single-center retrospective cohort studied women with mixed vulvar/vaginal pain treated with PBM/low-level laser therapy. Its patient-rated global responses are uncontrolled and cannot establish a PVD-specific effect (Plumasseau et al., 2026). A 2026 network meta-analysis reported pain benefit for a tissue-based category pooling PBM with low-level laser, vaginal TENS, and shockwave. The authors caution that this category-level estimate cannot be attributed to PBM alone; each modality is supported by only one to three trials (Spinillo et al., 2026).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for provoked vestibulodynia was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell, tissue or ex-vivo study directly tested provoked vestibulodynia.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2017 trial used 820-nm near-infrared light at 32 J/cm2, delivered by a focal probe to vestibular points for 12 sessions over six weeks. The 2025 study used a class III system with 660-nm red and 840-nm near-infrared array light, plus 660/825-nm focal-probe light, directed to vestibular, perineal, and sacral areas with individually progressed exposure over 15 sessions. Its abstract states eight weeks, while its methods state 12 weeks. The mapped 2026 cohort used an endovaginal probe for six to eight sessions. These protocols are not interchangeable and do not establish an optimal dose (Lev-Sagie et al., 2017; Antonio et al., 2025; Plumasseau et al., 2026).

Interpretation

Direct trials suggest short-term improvement on some provoked-pain measures, but effects vary by outcome and protocol. Patient-reported overall improvement and sexual-function outcomes were not clearly better than sham. The 2022 PVD review judged the earlier laser evidence very uncertain; the 2026 meta-analysis is supportive only at the pooled treatment-category level. Independent, adequately powered PBM trials with longer follow-up and validated function outcomes remain needed.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two small sham-controlled PVD trials report short-term benefit on some pain measures, but differ in outcomes and protocols. A 2022 PVD-specific systematic review rated the older trial's evidence very low certainty. A newer meta-analysis found benefit for a pooled category combining PBM with shockwave, TENS, and other low-level laser, but cautioned that the effect cannot be assigned to PBM alone; direct trials remain small and follow-up is limited.
